listings.name: Acropolis of Athens
listings.content: It was the ancient fortified town of Athens, dating back to the Late Bronze Age. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its historic role and the many iconic buildings of the Greek Classical age, among them the Parthenon, the Erectheion, and the Temple of Athena Nike. The key landmark of Athens, visible from afar, the Acropolis dominates the Athenian sky and symbolizes the foundation of modern culture and civilization. The Acropolis is considered to be an enduring symbol of Western civilisation.

listings.name: Propylaea
listings.content: The monumental gate at the western end of the Acropolis with Doric columns of Pentelic marble. In a prominent position on a steep bastion to the right of the entrance is the Temple of Athena Nike

listings.name: Parthenon
listings.content: This massive temple was built in the 5th century BC in thanksgiving for the Greek victory over Persian invaders. It was later converted into a Christian church, then an Ottoman mosque. It was mostly intact until 1687, when a Venetian bomb landed on the Parthenon, which the Ottomans had used as a munitions dump. From 1800 to 1803, the 7th Earl of Elgin removed many of the surviving sculptures and shipped them to England. Since 1975, numerous large-scale restoration projects have been undertaken to preserve remaining artefacts and ensure its structural integrity.

listings.name: Erectheion
listings.content: This elegant temple was primarily dedicated to the goddess Athena. The uneven ground led to a complex plan, with an east-facing entrance lined with six Ionic columns. Unusually, the temple has two porches, one borne by Ionic columns, the other supported by huge female caryatids.

listings.name: Theatre of Dionysus
listings.content: Classical Athens' main theatre, the first theatre ever built. Many of the great Greek plays were performed here for the first time. According to Plato's Symposium, it could hold an audience of 19,000 spectators. Aristophanes' The Clouds, mocking Socrates, was first performed here, and Plato considered this play to be a contributing factor in Socrates' trial and execution.

listings.name: Odeon of Herodes Atticus
listings.content: This theatre, built in 161 CE, is still used for concerts and plays. The stone backdrop is still preserved to a remarkable height of 3 stories, because it was incorporated into a later fortification on the site.

listings.name: Acropolis Museum
listings.content: You will need to purchase a timed-entry ticket for this museum, separate from the Acropolis. Buying online in advance from the official website is strongly recommended. This museum replaces an older museum on the Acropolis, which was far too small to hold and display all the artifacts recovered by archaeologists. Its design looks very "modern" from the outside, but on the inside it's very intuitive. The main floor is filled with a seemingly-endless collection of classical sculptures excavated from each stage of pre-Roman Athens. The top floor has an excellent view of the Acropolis and lavish placeholder exhibits for the Parthenon Marbles, to refute the United Kingdom's arrogant excuse that Greece did not have an appropriate place to display them. Most people will need at least one hour; anyone who loves classical art will need two hours or more. Exhibits have detailed descriptions, and the museum offers a free app-based audioguide. Archaeologists uncovered Roman ruins at the site before construction began; the final compromise was to elevate the museum above them. After you visit the museum, go down the path to the left of the main entrance plaza and use your museum ticket to access the Roman ruins.

listings.name: Pnyx
listings.content: If Athens is the birthplace of democracy, then Pnyx is its cradle. Around 507 BCE this rocky hill, overlooking the Akropolis, became the meeting place for the ekklesia, Athens' early democratic assembly. This site thus witnessed addresses by Pericles, Aristides and Alcibiades during the "Golden Age" of Athens, and had a capacity for 6000 to 13,000 hearers. The site was redesigned several times, creating three distinct phases in its history, until the ekklesia moved to the Theatre of Dionysos some time during the first century BCE. During the Roman era Pnyx was instead used as a sanctuary of Zeus.

listings.name: Ancient Agora
listings.content: The site of the ancient city centre is a green space with a beautiful view of the Acropolis. It was built as a multipurpose area, then evolved into a religious area over time. The Ancient Agora was eventually abandoned and then large parts of it were later built over for a thousand years. The open space you see today was excavated starting in the 1850s.
listings.price: €20, reduced €10, ticket valid for both the archaeological site and the museum

listings.name: Temple of Hephaestus
listings.content: The best preserved ancient Greek temple, 5th century BCE.

listings.name: Stoa of Attalus
listings.content: This building was reconstructed in the 1950s from its original foundations, incorporating as much of the original structure and materials as possible, with limestone quarried from Piraeus and roof tiles made of clay from Attica. It is used as a museum to house relics found in the Agora.

listings.name: Church of the Holy Apostles
listings.content: From the 11th century, one of the oldest churches in Athens.

listings.name: Roman Agora
listings.content: This area became the main marketplace of the city after the Ancient Agora to the west became primarily a religious facility under Roman rule. It houses the Tower of the Winds, an eight-sided tower with a different wind deity on each side, the remains of ancient shops, and a fountain. Although the official entrance faces the end of Pikilis, you cannot buy tickets at the entrance. The ticket office is just around the corner and across the street to the north, on Epaminonda.

listings.name: Kerameikos
listings.content: The site of the ancient cemetery of Athens. It also houses the Dipylon Gate, where the Panathenaic procession would begin. Its museum showcasing many of the grave stele and other archaeological items found on the grounds. The site has more than 20 tortoises, so be sure to watch your step and not trample on them.

listings.name: Temple of Olympian Zeus
listings.content: Only the ruins remain today. The column that has fallen and can still be seen in pieces was brought down during a thunderstorm about a century ago.

listings.name: Arch of Hadrian
listings.content: A monumental gateway resembling a Roman triumphal arch. It was built around 131 AD to honor the Roman emperor Hadrian, an admirer of Greek culture, for his many benefactions to the city.

listings.name: The Lyceum
listings.content: An ancient temple here hosted lectures by Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, and early meetings of the Athenian Assembly. Aristotle made the temple the home of his school, the Lyceum. It hosted the world's first zoo and botanical garden, as well as a library which preserved classical Greek works for centuries afterwards. Rediscovered in 1996, the site can now be viewed outdoors. Entrance is from the north, from the same entrance as for the Byzantine and Christian museum.

listings.name: Plato's Academy
listings.content: This house of study was founded by the famous philosopher Plato. His equally famous follower Aristotle studied here for 20 years before leaving to found a school of his own. The site is an outdoor free park where you can see the excavated ruins. The ruins are not well explained or particularly impressive, but they do form a very nice park in a charming family oriented neighborhood. The exact coordinates given here are for a sign which best explains the various ruins in the park. The site is a long walk from all other historic sites, or a single bus route which runs slower than walking on the busy streets.

listings.name: Hadrian's Reservoir
listings.content: Now the base of a summertime outdoor cinema, you can view the remains of the reservoir that was the terminus of an aqueduct that transported water for Roman-era Athenians from Parnitha to the base of Mount Lycabettus. You can only peer through windows and are not able to descend into the reservoir.

listings.name: Panathinaiko Stadium
listings.content: The stadium that housed the first modern day Olympic Games of 1896. Earlier versions of the stadium date as far back as 330 BCE. It's an enormous, white, marble stadium, with a horseshoe configuration.

listings.name: Lycabettus Hill
listings.content: A 200m hill bordering the Kolonaki district. You can reach the top by walking (the path starts 15 minutes from Evangelismos metro stop, and will take 30 minutes to walk up the winding, but paved and not steep, path) or by a funicular railway (€10 single/€13 return trip). From halfway up looking towards the sea there are astonishing views of the Parthenon with the blue of the sea glimpsed between its columns. And from the top you can see the whole city, the port of Piraeus and, on a clear day, the island of Aegina and the Peloponnese. Have a drink at the cafe there, and visit the chapel of St George.

listings.name: National Theatre
listings.content: A low but imposing building erected between 1882 and 1890 by architect Ernst Ziller in the eclectic style of that age, commissioned by King George I.

listings.name: Syntagma Square
listings.content: Check out the Parliament building and the newly restored Grande Bretagne Hotel.

listings.name: Hellenic Parliament Building
listings.content: This building is on the eastern side of the square. It was the former royal palace before Greece became a republic. At its base, facing the square, is the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

listings.name: Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
listings.content: Catch the changing of the guards in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in front of Parliament every hour on the hour. The guards are a fascinating sight; they wear distinctive uniforms with pleated kilts and leather clogs with pom-poms. The uniforms and the guards' unusual marching style are a tribute to the light infantry insurgents (evzones) who bravely fought the Greek War of Independence. Make sure you don't get too close or stand on the wrong side of them if you want to take a picture. If that occurs, they will knock their gun and, as they are not allowed to speak, another guard in regular military uniform will kindly ask you to change position. A more elaborate version of the ceremony takes place at 11:00 every Sunday, when it is accompanied by a marching military band.

listings.name: Daphni Monastery
listings.content: An 11th-century Byzantine monastery and UNESCO World Heritage site. Damaged by an earthquake in 1999, but has now been fully restored.

listings.name: Kaisariani Monastery and Gardens
listings.content: A nice escape from the city in the foothills of Mount Hymettus. Walking trails. There's a functional monastery one can walk in, and several ruined chapels or basilicas up on the walks.

listings.name: National Archaeological Museum of Athens
listings.content: This is the largest and most popular of Athens' many museums, and is usually very crowded. Its vast collection includes treasures unearthed from Mycenae by Heinrich Schliemann; a staggering array of sculpture including the earliest known Greek figurines dating from around 2,000 BCE; frescoes from the volcanic island of Santorini; and remains of Antikythera mechanism, the oldest known mechanical computer. Plan to make several visits to absorb it all.

listings.name: Kanellopoulos Museum
listings.content: A small but excellent museum displays artifacts from Mycenean Greece on, and includes some wonderful Persian artifacts.

listings.name: Benaki Museum of Greek Culture
listings.content: Visit the beautiful Neoclassical main building which houses collections of Greek art, from ancient times through the Byzantine period and the modern state. Open late and for free on Thursday evenings. The museum shop is a good place to buy souvenirs. There is a small selection at high prices but the quality is excellent.
listings.price: €9, students, seniors, people with disabilities and teachers €7; temporary exhibitions €7/€5; €25 Benaki Museum Experience ticket entitles the visitor to one entrance per exhibition in all the Benaki Museum buildings, valid for 3 months

listings.name: Museum of Cycladic Art
listings.content: Holds the second largest collection of Cypriot antiquities in the world outside Cyprus, after the Metropolitan Museum in New York. Some of the most popular exhibits include the Cycladic figurines, the idols from Early Bronze Age Cyclades, whose style greatly influenced modernist work in the 20th century, and Cypriot pottery and Ancient Greek artifacts, especially the ‘Scenes of Daily Life in Ancient Greece’ display, which is popular with families. They also sell great souvenirs, and lunch is available at the elegant Aethrion Café. If you are lucky, there may be a quirky temporary exhibition too (with no extra entry fee), as they hold archaeological, modern and contemporary art exhibitions.

listings.name: National Gallery
listings.content: It's one of Greece's main art institutions and features paintings and works of art from some of Greece's and Europe's best from the 19th and 20th centuries. Emphasis is given to popular Greek contemporary artists including Giannis Tsarouchis, Domenikos Theotokopoulos (a.k.a. El Greco), Theodors Vrizakis, Nikolaos Kounelakis, Nikiforos Litras, Konstantinos Parthenis, Maleas, Giannis Moralis and others.

listings.name: Benaki Museum of Islamic Art
listings.content: An excellent collection which anyone interested in Islamic art will want to see. The museum was opened in 2004 as a branch of the Benaki, but is in a different part of town in two connected buildings.

listings.name: Museum of Greek Folk Art
listings.content: An excellent museum of its type. Too often neglected by visitors to Athens, even though it is in the heavily touristed Plaka neighbourhood. Displays include artefacts, tools, primitive painting, folk pottery and interior decor. It is particularly strong on costume and embroidery.
listings.price: €2; students from non–EU countries, senior citizens from EU €1; under 19, students from EU (with ID), and people with disabilities free

listings.name: Athens Municipal Art Gallery
listings.content: Paintings of Greek painters of the first half of the 20th century are displayed.

listings.name: Vorres Museum
listings.content: A museum of folk and contemporary art. Its grounds cover 320,000 m2 (80 acres) including several buildings, gardens and courtyards. Its collection includes over 6,000 pieces covering 4,000 years of Greek history and art. The museum was donated by the Vorres family to the Greek state.
listings.address: 1 Parodos Diadochou Constantinou St., Paiania, Attiki

listings.name: Museum of Ancient Greek Technology Kotsanas
listings.content: A very interesting museum that should not be missed. Excellent demonstration of some fantastic inventions of the ancient Greeks. Most models are functional and can be interacted with. Some can only be interacted with when a docent is leading a tour, so join one as soon as you can. Upstairs is a display of ancient Greek musical instruments—some of them playable, and downstairs is a display of reproductions of ancient Greek armor. It's a relatively small museum, but if you take the time to read everything, it will take several hours.

listings.name: National Historical Museum
listings.content: In the old parliament building, this museum contains a large collection of historic documents such as the first constitution of Greece, furniture, equipment from the revolution. If you are lucky you may see the old session room.

listings.name: Numismatic Museum
listings.content: The building of the museum is one of the most beautiful in Athens, and was built by Ernst Ziller and was used as the residence in Athens of Schliemann. The collection contains thousands of ancient coins and ancient Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Medieval figurines.

listings.name: Museum of Greek Popular Musical Instruments
listings.content: Includes exhibits of traditional Greek musical instruments, with recordings of most of them.

listings.name: National War Museum
listings.content: The National War Museum is the only significant surviving public project of the military dictatorship which ruled Greece 1967 - 1974. The museum's displays are old fashioned and biased towards the more successful periods of Greek military history. The tanks, artillery guns and aircraft on display outside the museum form the most interesting part of its collection, and can be visited for free. Perhaps the only internationally famous object in the collection is the portrait of Lord Byron in hellenic dress.

listings.name: Park of Maritime Tradition
listings.content: Including the historical warships Georgios Averof, Velos and a replica of an ancient trireme.

listings.name: Hellenic Air Force Museum
listings.content: A number of old planes from as far back as the 1930s can be seen here.

listings.name: City of Athens Technopolis
listings.content: An industrial museum of incomparable architecture. The centre has assisted in the upgrading of a historic Athens district.

listings.name: Spathario Museum
listings.content: The first and unique museum of shadow theatre in the world, dedicated to the famous Greek shadow theatre character "Karagiozis".

listings.name: Planetary Evgenidio Foundation
listings.address: 387 Syggrou Ave. (entrance 11 Pentelis st Palaio Faliro, Athens 175 64)

listings.name: National Gardens
listings.content: A Peaceful and beautiful park in the centre of Athens, easily the coolest place to hide from the summer sun. Wander around, check out the quirky art that seems to sprout up every now and again, look on in disbelief at the "zoo", sit on one of the benches, enjoy the luxuriant flowers and vegetation, marvel at the turtle and duck ponds, have a frappe in the cafe, and spot one of the resident tortoises exploring... it's a fun place to hang out.

listings.name: Pedion tou Areos
listings.content: Covers 27.7 hectares, near the National Archaeological Museum.

listings.name: Dionysiou Aeropagitou Street
listings.content: This landmark street starts from the Temple of Olympian Zeus at Vasilissis Olgas Avenue, continues under the southern slopes of the Acropolis near Plaka, and finishes just beyond the Temple of Hephaestus in Thiseio. The street has been pedestrianised, forming a scenic route. The entire route provides visitors with views of the Parthenon and the Agora (the meeting point of ancient Athenians), away from the busy city centre.

listings.name: Parnitha National Park
listings.content: Well-marked paths, gorges, springs, torrents and caves do the protected area. Hiking and mountain-biking in all four mountains remain popular outdoor activities for many residents of the city.

listings.name: Athens Festival
listings.content: Runs from May to October each year. Offers a wide spectrum of events covering almost every taste. Outside Athens, try to attend a performance at the ancient theater of Epidaurus – a truly unforgettable experience.

listings.name: Athens Concert Hall
listings.content: This venue attracts world-famous artists all year round.

listings.name: Stavros Niarchos Cultural Centre
listings.content: This complex in the seaside suburb of Kallithea has stunning views from its terrace all the way to the Acropolis on one side and of the coast on the other. Evening concerts and other cultural events take place here. The building, gardens and complex alone are worth a visit, and a free shuttle bus is provided from Syntagma Square. Check the web site for the free (optional) tours in English. The collection of the National Library of Greece is being transferred here, and one wing of the building contains an opera house (this part can only be visited as part of a free tour, if you are not attending an event in the auditorium).

listings.name: Σουβλάκι Κώστας 1950 συνταγμα (Kostas)
listings.content: It's authentic, friendly and fast.

listings.name: The 2 Brothers
listings.content: The best souvlaki in this part of Athens.

listings.name: Vegan Beat Athens
listings.content: Vegan street food restaurant. Tasty food and nice people that work there. A good place for all vegans and even non-vegans. The true Parthenon of the vegan scene of Athens. Excellent vegan souvlaki.

listings.name: The Traditional
listings.content: Traditional Greek food. If you want to eat in a quality village tavern in the center of Athens, you will come here. Great roasted food, salads and appetizers! The food is handmade.

listings.name: Krasopoulio tou Kokkora
listings.content: Among the best traditional Greek restaurants in Athens downtown. The owner is smiling, polite and very keen to assist. A wonderful casual lunch or dinner spot. Fresh ingredients and substantial portions.

listings.name: Aspro Alogo
listings.content: An excellent little Greek restaurant well worth finding. Everything is fresh and delicious and the service is great. The owner is a helpful and generous guy. Attentive and familiar treatment.

listings.name: Atlantikos
listings.content: Nice little place with great seafood selection. The meals look simple and are delicious. The portions are quite large and the quality price ratio is very well balanced. One should go in time and expect quite some waiting time to get a table on a small alley. Best local fish tavern with crunchy anchovies and perfect frying without being oily.

listings.name: Kafeneio Ivis
listings.content: Very authentic Greek tavern, frequented by locals. Great value for money. Warm welcome, nice terrace and fast service.

listings.name: Lefka
listings.content: A long-established traditional taverna with spacious outdoor seating. Closed Sundays.

listings.name: K Filippou
listings.content: A long-established taverna serving some of the best and most authentic food in Athens. Seating is indoors and outdoors, though it's hard to find a seat in the latter during pleasant weather.

listings.name: Karamanlidika
listings.content: A very remarkable, slightly upscale restaurant specializing in dishes native to the Karamanli people. Owing to their history, the food served here is a (very well-executed) mix between Greek and Turkish cuisine. A hidden gem (that is rather crowded, though)! Expect to pay 11€ per person for main courses and water.

listings.name: Karavitis
listings.content: a severely traditional taverna where the speciality is stamnaki, or beef, potatoes and cheese cooked in tomato sauce in an individual clay pot. The fried zucchini here are also always good. Mostly patronized by Greeks, but there is an English-language menu.

listings.name: Το Κιούπι (To Kioupi)
listings.content: Known among some expatriates as "the hole in the ground," this is a basement taverna serving authentic, inexpensive traditional Greek fare.

listings.name: Platanos Taverna
listings.content: One of the oldest tavernas in Plaka with a pleasant outdoor terrace under a huge plane tree, though some old Athens hands have complained that the food has become lacklustre.

listings.name: Zeus Xenios
listings.content: literally in the shadow of the Acropolis, offers quieter and less expensive dining than the many touristy tavernas lining Mnesikleous whose touts will try to snare you as you walk up the hill. The view isn't as spectacular as you might expect, but the outdoor seating is very pleasant and the traditional Greek dishes include some unusual ones, like grilled peppers in yogurt sauce. The price includes a bottle of water, an appetizer plate and garlic bread.

listings.name: Pame Psirri
listings.content: On Agii Anargiri square -- Psiri. A "mezedopolio" where local singers sing rempetika music.

listings.name: O Morias
listings.content: Greek restaurant

listings.name: Voskopoula (The Shepherdess)
listings.content: Greek restaurant

listings.name: Τaverna Μanolis.
listings.content: Greek restaurant taverna.

listings.name: Rosalia
listings.content: A tavern that serves simple, traditional Greek meals.

listings.name: Giántes
listings.content: A tavern with a garden serving organic dishes.

listings.name: Orea Penteli
listings.content: Another "mezedopolio" with live music in an old restored building.

listings.name: Cafe Avissinia
listings.content: A remarkable restaurant, serving refined and creative innovations on traditional Greek dishes in a chic setting. It is on the square of the same name which is the venue of the main Athens flea market. This is an interesting place to come for lunch, where you can sit enjoying the upscale food and ambiance while looking out on the gritty bazaar of the Flea Market. Moderately expensive, and unfortunately no open wine, though they do have a short but well-chosen list of Greek bottled wines. Open for lunch and dinner. Those considering walking there for dinner from Plaka or the Monastiraki Metro should be aware that the intervening area, while fine by day and not known to be particularly dangerous even at night, it does take on an uncomfortable "Bladerunner" atmosphere after dark.

listings.name: Balux
listings.content: One of the best bars in Athens for the specific style, to call it a bar is an understatement. Balux is large complex set right on the water in Glyfada, one of the trendiest areas of the city. It is open during the summer for swimming in the ocean or pool all day and turns into a lounge and full club at night. Where Athens' wealthy go to party.
listings.address: Vassileos Georgiou B No. 58 Asteria, Glyfada

listings.name: Rebetiki Istoria
listings.content: One of the best rebetica clubs, often open in summer when most others are closed.

listings.name: Showroom
listings.content: Nice cafe/restaurant.

listings.name: Ydria
listings.content: This sprawling cafe-restaurant that takes up a large part of Platía Paliás Agorás along Adhrianoú St. at the western end of Plaka, is a good place for daytime coffee or a before or after dinner drink. They also serve food, though if you're there for a meal you'll be directed to a different seating area, so tell the waiter when you arrive if you just want a drink. This is the most pleasant cafe in a square packed with them; despite the Plaka location it's relatively quiet, with snatches of views of antiquity from the mostly outdoor seating. Particularly popular with younger Greeks, though all ages and nationalities will feel comfortable. Prices average or slightly below for Plaka, which still means not cheap, though the ouzo comes in hefty shots, and if you order the giant "ouzo platter" (€25) of appetizers with them, it will easily suffice for three people.

listings.name: Costa
listings.content: Standard stuff, but has a nice air conditioned and quiet upstairs seating area overlooking the square.

listings.name: Metamatic_taf
listings.content: Independent space organising and hosting cultural events related to all forms of artistic production, and a point of social gathering. Great cocktails and a variety of jazz/soul music.

listings.name: Playce
listings.content: A really nice cafe where you can play board games whilst drinking your coffee. Very popular.

listings.name: Filion Cafe
listings.content: Start the day with a double shot of dark espresso at this cafe in the Kolonaki neighbourhood, just north of Syntagma Square.

listings.name: Dionissotis Camping
listings.content: It has a hall for breakfast, a minimarket, a swimming pool and a playground for the children. 115 places for tents.
listings.price: €6 per person, €4 per small tent, €6 per large tent/caravan

listings.name: Athens Backpackers
listings.content: Standard backpacking hostel offering clean and comfortable beds, 24 hr reception access, and discounted wifi access. Great spot to meet other travellers.

listings.name: Athens Psiri Hotel
listings.content: Fully renovated in 2020. All rooms include private bathrooms, free wifi, air conditioning and heating.

listings.name: Safestay Athens Monastiraki
listings.content: Studios and hostel beds within walking distance of the metro. Each dorm has lockers. Artists have painted murals in the reception and some of the rooms, and there's a basement lounge with art exhibitions, pool table, home cimena and internet corner. The small rooftop bar is ideal for evening drinks. It produces a weekly art and culture guide. Yellow and green building.

listings.name: Hotel Dioskouros Athens
listings.content: Offers simple clean accommodation in a central location.

listings.name: Hostel Aprodite
listings.content: Low-budget backpackers' hangout not too far from Larissa train station and Victoria Square, a bit north of the Omonia district.
listings.price: €12 for a 6 bed dorm, €14 for a 4 bed dorm, and more. Air conditioning €3 extra per person
listings.address: 12 Einardou and Michail Voda corner 65, Athena 10440, Greece

listings.name: Orion
listings.content: This small hotel is next to Strefi hill, offers nice view from its terrace and is in a calm area. Freshly renovated rooms and breakfast in communal kitchen. Internet included and sister hotel offers nice breakfast at the terrace, too.

listings.name: Hotel Elite Athens
listings.content: 10 minutes walk from Monastiraki; simple, decorated rooms with air conditioning and TV. There is also a bar and coffee shop on the ground floor.

listings.name: Acropolis View Hotel Athens
listings.content: Attention to detail is catered for in this hotel, with most rooms having a fresh lick of paint on them every year. Rooms have central heating and A/C, private baths and mini fridges, and some have balconies. Price from €88 for a single room in high season.

listings.name: Hotel Acropolis House
listings.content: The staff are very friendly and the hotel will hold your luggage if you are departing later in the day. Some of the older, more expensive rooms are very atmospheric; others are rather drab.

listings.name: Athos
listings.content: Patrou 3. Nice hotel in Plaka with roof-garden with a view of the Acropolis.

listings.name: Central Hotel
listings.content: Designed by architect Stelios Demos, this hotel fuses modern art design with a classical Greek touch. Restaurant, daily buffet breakfast. Priced from €128 for a standard room in the high season.

listings.name: O&B Athens Boutique Hotel
listings.content: A small boutique hotel in the center of Athens, close to sightseeing, shopping, and entertainment.

listings.name: Hotel Omiros Athens
listings.content: Each of the 40 rooms features air conditioning, a television and a mini fridge.

listings.name: Fresh Hotel
listings.content: A superb designer hotel within easy walking distance of the Acropolis in the centre of Athens. The rooftop bar and swimming pool has breathtaking views of the Acropolis - the perfect way to end the day's sightseeing or business.

listings.name: Periscope Hotel
listings.content: An upscale (with prices to match) hip boutique hotel in Kolonaki with glossy, minimalist decor. This hotel used to be the Athenian Inn, and that name may still be found in some Athens hotel listings in guidebooks, but the former hotel has been so completely refurbished that it is now a totally different establishment.

listings.name: Radisson Blu Park Hotel
listings.content: 5 star hotel offering high speed internet access and express mail, late check out and foreign currency exchange.

listings.name: The St George Lycabettus Hotel Athens
listings.content: Located in Kolonaki. This boutique hotel offers great views of the Acropolis.

listings.name: Conrad Athens the Ilisian
listings.content: Just south of the Kolonaki district, this is the biggest hotel with the biggest pool in Athens. Fifteen floors and wonderful views everywhere you look. Also the "Milos Restaurant" is on site.

listings.name: President Hotel Athens
listings.content: A 4-star hotel renovated in 2004 with a lovely terrace bar and pool, 3 restaurants with view of the Lycabetus hill, and very accommodating personnel. The hotel is in an ideal location for catching the bus or the metro for the north suburbs of Athens (Kifisia, Marousi, Chalandri etc). Acropolis, Lycabetus hill, Syntagma square are all within 5 to 15 min taxi drive.
listings.price: ~€80 per night for a double bed room

listings.name: Royal Olympic Hotel
listings.content: In front of the Temple of Zeus. Outdoor swimming pool, rooftop garden restaurant. Free wi fi and conference room available.

listings.name: Electra Hotel
listings.content: A 4-star property in the heart of Athens. Within walking distance from all major historical sites and the business and commercial districts.

listings.name: Grande Bretagne Hotel
listings.content: Traditionally the "best hotel in town," this historic luxury hotel with gilded woods, fine fabrics and chandeliers in the public areas has long been the accommodation of choice for visiting diplomats and power players.

listings.name: King George Palace
listings.content: Some rooms have a view of the Acropolis, and the Royal Presidential Suite has a private outdoor pool. The Tudor restaurant on the 7th floor has views of the Acropolis.
listings.address: 3 Vassileos Georgiou A' St, Syntagma Square

listings.name: Hellenic Vibes
listings.content: Hellenic Vibes Smart Hotel is a brand new 5-star hotel right in the heart of rebranded Athens, with a capacity of 35 rooms and exclusive suites, is located behind the doors of an impressive neoclassical facade of the 19th century.

places.title: Acropolis Museum
places.blurb: The Acropolis Museum is an archaeological museum focused on the findings of the archaeological site of the Acropolis of Athens.

places.title: Agios Panteleimonas, Athens
places.blurb: Agios Panteleimonas or Aghios Panteleimonas is a neighbourhood of Athens, located northwest of the centre of Athens between Viktoria Square and Attikis Square.

places.title: Akadimia Platonos
places.blurb: Akadimia Platonos literally meaning Plato's Academy, is a neighbourhood located 3 km west-northwest of the downtown part of the Greek capital of Athens.

places.title: Alexandras Avenue
places.blurb: Alexandra's Avenue is a main east–west thoroughfare running from Patission Street/28 October Street and Kifissias Avenue in the northern part of the center of Athens, Greece.

places.title: Agoraios Kolonos
places.blurb: Agoraios Kolonos, located to the south and adjacently situated on a hill near the Temple of Hephaestus, used to be the meeting place of the ancient Athenian craftsmen.

places.title: Aglaureion
places.blurb: The Aglaureion, or the Sanctuary of Aglauros, was an ancient sanctuary located in the Acropolis in Athens, Greece.

places.title: Akadimia, Athens
places.blurb: Akadimia, literally "Academy", is a neighborhood in central Athens, Greece.

places.title: Agios Eleftherios, Athens
places.blurb: Agios Eleftherios is a neighborhood of the center of Athens, Greece.

places.title: Aerides, Athens
places.blurb: Aerides is a small neighborhood of the center of Athens, Greece surrounding the Tower of the Winds, from where it takes its name.

places.title: Alekos Fassianos Museum
places.blurb: The Alekos Fassianos Museum, is an art museum in Athens, Greece, dedicated to the life and multifaceted work of the Greek painter Alekos Fassianos.

places.title: Temple of Olympian Zeus, Athens
places.blurb: The Temple of Olympian Zeus, also known as the Olympieion or Columns of the Olympian Zeus, is a colossal temple in the centre of Athens, now in ruins.

places.title: Parthenon
places.blurb: The Parthenon is a former temple on the Athenian Acropolis, Greece, that was dedicated to the goddess Athena.

places.title: Mount Lycabettus
places.blurb: Mount Lycabettus, also known as Lycabettos, Lykabettos or Lykavittos, is a Cretaceous limestone hill in the Greek capital Athens.

places.title: Erechtheion
places.blurb: The Erechtheion or Temple of Athena Polias is an ancient Greek Ionic temple, on the north side of the Acropolis, Athens, that was primarily dedicated to the goddess Athena.

places.title: Tower of the Winds
places.blurb: The Tower of the Winds, known as the Ωρολόγιο του Κυρρήστου in Greek, and by other names, is an octagonal Pentelic marble tower in the Roman Agora in Athens, named after the eight large reliefs of wind gods around its…

places.title: Pnyx
places.blurb: The Pnyx is a hill or hillside in central Athens, the capital of Greece.

places.title: Temple of Athena Nike
places.blurb: The Temple of Athena Nike, the smallest temple on the Acropolis of Athens, is dedicated to the goddesses Athena and Nike.

places.title: Ancient Agora of Athens
places.blurb: The Ancient Agora of Athens is an ancient Greek agora.

places.title: Panathenaic Stadium
places.blurb: The Panathenaic Stadium or Kallimarmaro is a multi-purpose stadium in Athens, Greece.

places.title: Theatre of Dionysus
places.blurb: The Theatre of Dionysus is an ancient Greek theatre in Athens.

places.title: Odeon of Herodes Atticus
places.blurb: The Odeon of Herodes Atticus is a stone Greek theatre structure located on the southwest slope of the Acropolis of Athens, Greece.

places.title: Choragic Monument of Lysicrates
places.blurb: The Choragic Monument of Lysicrates near the Acropolis of Athens was erected by the choregos Lysicrates, a wealthy patron of musical performances in the Theater of Dionysus, to commemorate the prize in the dithyramb c…

places.title: Syntagma Square
places.blurb: Syntagma Square is the central square of Athens, Greece.

places.title: Arch of Hadrian
places.blurb: The Arch of Hadrian, most commonly known in Greek as Hadrian's Gate, is a monumental gateway resembling—in some respects—a Roman triumphal arch.

places.title: National Archaeological Museum, Athens
places.blurb: The National Archaeological Museum in Athens houses some of the most important artifacts from a variety of archaeological locations around Greece from prehistory to late antiquity.

places.title: Archaeological Society of Athens
places.blurb: The Archaeological Society of Athens is an independent learned society.

places.title: Athena Promachos
places.blurb: The Athena Promachos was a colossal bronze statue of Athena sculpted by Phidias, which stood between the Propylaea and the Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens.

places.title: National Garden, Athens
places.blurb: The National Garden, formerly known as the Royal Garden until 1974, is a public park of 15.5 hectares in the center of the Greek capital, Athens.

places.title: Presidential Mansion, Athens
places.blurb: The Presidential Mansion in Athens, Greece, is the official residence of the president of the Hellenic Republic.

places.title: Kaisariani Monastery
places.blurb: The Kaisariani Monastery is an Eastern Orthodox monastery built on the north side of Mount Hymettus, near Athens, Greece.

places.title: Athens Concert Hall
places.blurb: The Athens Concert Hall is a concert hall located on Vasilissis Sofias Avenue in Athens, Greece.

places.title: National Gallery
places.blurb: The National Gallery is an art museum located on Vasilissis Sofias avenue in the Pangrati district, Athens, Greece.

places.title: Byzantine and Christian Museum
places.blurb: The Byzantine and Christian Museum is situated at Vassilissis Sofias Avenue in Athens, Greece.

places.title: Athens War Museum
places.blurb: The Athens War Museum is the military museum of the Greek Armed Forces.

places.title: Goulandris Museum of Cycladic Art
places.blurb: The Nikolaos P. Goulandris Foundation - Museum of Cycladic Art is a museum in Athens that houses a notable collection of artifacts of Cycladic art.

places.title: Numismatic Museum of Athens
places.blurb: The Numismatic Museum of Athens is one of the most important museums in Greece, holding a collection of over 500,000 coins, medals, engraved gems, weights, stamps and related artefacts from 1400 BC to modern times.

places.title: Tactual Museum of Athens
places.blurb: The Tactual Museum of Athens is a museum for the visually impaired in Kallithea, Athens, Greece.

places.title: National Historical Museum, Athens
places.blurb: The National Historical Museum is a historical museum in Athens.

places.title: Nordic Library at Athens
places.blurb: The Nordic Library at Athens is one of several international archaeological libraries in Athens, Greece.
